title: Living well with dementia | NHS inform
text:
Living well with dementia
People can, and do, live a good life with dementia for years. Because dementia is progressive and affects different people in different ways, it’s important to continue to do what matters to you and for your life.
Keep socialising
If you have dementia, it’s helpful to keep in touch with people and take part in social activities. It can keep you active and stimulated.
You could:
go to the cinema or theatre
join a walking group
take part in a choir
There are
dementia friendly groups
, communities, sport and cultural activities that support people living with dementia to be active as the dementia symptoms progress.
These groups also support care partners and families to participate and share experiences.
This can be a good way to share experiences and get useful tips from people who have been through something similar.
Look after your overall health
Living a healthy lifestyle is important for everyone, including people with dementia.
Do
eat a healthy, balanced diet
drink plenty of fluids
exercise regularly – this could be a daily walk, gardening, or you could a movement class
get enough sleep – try to avoid naps during the day
avoid caffeine and alcohol at night
have regular dental, eyesight and hearing check-ups
Music can also help dementia symptoms as it may stimulate memory.
Playlist for Life
have advice on making a playlist for someone with dementia.
If you have a long-term condition like
diabetes
or
heart disease
, try to attend regular check-ups with your GP.
If you feel unwell, speak to your GP. Things like chest or urine infections can make you feel very confused if they’re not treated quickly.
Depression
is common in dementia. You should talk to your GP about this as there are talking treatments that can help.
NHS inform also has general advice on managing your
mental health
and
wellbeing
like:
breathing and relaxation exercises
mindfulness for mental wellbeing
getting help with your mental health
You can also get support through
mental health services at NHS 24
and
Mind to Mind
.
Practical advice on living with dementia
Dementia can affect all aspects of life. If you’ve been diagnosed with dementia, it’s important to remember that:
you’re still you, even though you have problems with memory, concentration and planning
everyone experiences dementia differently
focusing on the things you can still do and enjoy will help you to stay positive
With the right help and support when you need it, many people can, and do, live well with dementia for many years.
More about everyday living with dementia
Money and legal matters
Age Scotland has information about
money advice and benefits you might be entitled to
.
They also have information about
legal matters like making a will and power of attorney
.
Work and dementia
Coping at work can be worrying if you have dementia.
You should speak to your employer about your dementia diagnosis as soon as you feel ready. You may be able to change your workload if you want to return to work, or continue to work. Employers can make reasonable adjustments that support you to stay at work.
You can also get advice from:
the disability employment advisor at your
local job centre
your trade union
your local Citizens Advice Bureau
If you decide to leave work, get advice about your pensions and benefits.
Driving and dementia
Many people with dementia are able to continue driving for some time. To continue driving, you must tell the
Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA)
that you have dementia.
The DVLA will ask for medical reports. They may also ask you to do a special driving assessment to decide whether you can continue driving.
People with dementia must give up driving when their symptoms become bad enough to make them unsafe on the road. This is to protect themselves, their passengers and other road users.
More about driving and dementia
Equipment and dementia
Equipment is available if you have dementia. For example, you may be able to get:
simplified mobile phones
smart watches that include GPS
everyday digital tools
like smart lighting and an easy TV remote
an using an
Alexa to help you with everyday tasks
living aids – like special utensils to help you eat and drink
telecare
– sensors or detectors that automatically send a signal to a carer or monitoring centre by telephone
More about equipment and dementia
Living at home with dementia
In the early stages of dementia, many people are able to look after their homes in the way they did before their diagnosis. But, as the illness gets worse, someone with dementia may need help with daily activities. For example, housework and shopping.
If you have dementia, your home may also need to be adapted. This is to keep you safe, mobile and independent.
Information about aids and adaptations for your home are available from your local council.
Read more about care equipment and adapting your home
Living alone with dementia
Many people with dementia continue to live on their own for some time. But, as your condition progresses, it’s likely you’ll need extra support to help you cope. It’s better to get this in place early.
Talk to family, friends and health professionals about how they can help you to stay independent. They can advise on how to cope with practical tasks, like shopping.
Your care and support options
As your dementia symptoms progress your health or social care professional can help to identify the right kind of support for you and the people looking after you.
They’ll find out what kind of support you need from your health and social care partnership. This can include things like:
equipment
self directed support
social care support from home
a stay in a care home
Making an advance care plan
An advance care plan allows you to state what you’d prefer in your medical treatment and care options. It can include:
what treatment you would consider, and in what circumstances
what types of treatment you would never want to have, no matter what the circumstances
what type of end of life care you would wish to have – for example, whether you would want to be resuscitated by artificial means
whether you would be willing to donate organs after your death
You cannot request anything illegal in your advance decision, like assisted suicide.
Your care team will be able to provide you with more information and advice about advance decisions.
